bridge: You know URLs, network routes and server APIs. Use the supplied fictional fetch-service diagram and authorised lab.
teaching:
### Follow whose network access is used

A browser requesting a URL uses the browser's network position. A server fetching that URL uses the server's position and permissions. It may reach internal services unavailable to the user.

A preview, import or image-fetching feature can therefore become an unintended bridge into a private network. The important question is which destinations the feature is meant to reach.

### Define allowed destinations

Prefer a small trusted destination set when the feature permits it. Parse URLs with an appropriate parser, allow only required schemes and restrict the final destination. Check address resolution, redirects and alternate address forms under the actual client library.

Validating one hostname string is insufficient if later resolution or a redirect sends the request somewhere else. A change between checking a name and using it is another timing problem to consider.

### Limit what a fetch can do

Use network restrictions, limited credentials, timeouts and response-size limits. Prevent the fetch worker from inheriting broad internal access simply because it runs on a server.

### Check the final connection

For each harmless lab case, record the requested URL, redirects, resolved destination and allowed outcome. A blocked spelling of one private address does not establish that the destination policy holds for every route.
example:
Synthetic allowlist: https://docs.example on port 443, no redirects
A: https://docs.example/help       -> allow
B: https://docs.example.evil.example/help -> deny
C: http://docs.example/help        -> deny scheme
D: https://docs.example:444/help    -> deny port
E: allowed A redirects elsewhere   -> reject redirect under this policy
explanation: The host in B is the longer name ending evil.example, not docs.example. Parsing separates scheme, authority and path; string containment does not. This fixture assumes destination resolution is also constrained by a separate egress policy, which must be verified in a real deployment.
exercise: Classify all five supplied cases and add https://other.example/docs.example as a sixth. Explain which component of each URL determines the allowlist comparison.
solution: Only A is allowed; the sixth is denied because its host is other.example. A path containing an allowed name does not change the destination authority.
challenge: Design a link-preview service supporting only two fixed documentation hosts. State redirect, timeout, size, credential and egress policies. Give a negative case for each boundary without making network requests.
challenge_solution: One paper design allows only HTTPS on port 443 for docs.example and help.example, no redirects, no forwarded user cookies or authorisation headers, a 3-second total request deadline and a 1 MB response cap. A separately enforced egress policy restricts actual destinations, including after DNS resolution, and blocks internal-only services. Negative cases: another hostname, port 444, a redirect even from an allowed host, an oversize response, a deadline overrun, or attempted credential forwarding all fail closed. These illustrative limits are policy choices, not universal production settings. No network request is needed to evaluate the cases.
